{"schema":"voice-draft-source/4","kind":"draft","draft":"# Choice screens are not market choice.

A choice screen is usually presented as a simple remedy: put several services in front of people and let them pick. Supporters can call that competition because the screen displays multiple logos. But the visible moment of choice comes after a series of less visible decisions—decisions about who appears, where each option appears, and what happens after the selection. A menu can offer alternatives while leaving control of the restaurant with the same owner.

Start with the list. Someone sets the eligibility rules (the company operating the screen), decides which applicants satisfy them, and determines how many options fit. Those choices can favor firms with particular technical resources, business models, or existing scale. A service excluded from the list cannot compete for the user at all. A service admitted only after accepting restrictive terms isn’t entering an open market; it’s entering a space whose gatekeeper still writes the conditions.

Placement matters too. The first item, the largest button, and the option requiring the fewest steps are not merely decorations (the order itself is a decision). If one service is already selected, people must notice the setting, understand it, and take action to change it. That friction may be small, but it points in one direction—toward the default. What good is a list of alternatives if the design quietly tells you which answer is expected?

Defaults also extend beyond the first click. Choosing a service may not change every related setting (a browser, assistant, or app store can have several separate defaults). Links may continue opening through the gatekeeper’s product. Prompts may repeatedly invite a switch back. Some functions may work better with the preferred option because access to system features is unequal. The screen says “choice,” but the surrounding product can make one answer durable and every other answer provisional.

That’s how nominal choice can preserve gatekeeper power. The gatekeeper still defines the candidates, controls the presentation, and owns the route through which competitors reach people. It can also observe which options gain traction (subject to applicable privacy rules) and revise the interface accordingly. The market is supposedly happening on the screen—yet the most consequential market decisions were made before the screen appeared.

A meaningful remedy does not stop at requiring more logos. It changes who controls eligibility and how the options are presented. Neutral criteria should not depend on accepting unrelated commercial terms. Ranking should rotate or follow a method the gatekeeper can’t manipulate (randomization is one possible method). No option should arrive preselected, and changing a default should be as easy as keeping it. The remedy must reach the entire path, including later prompts and settings (the interface after selection matters too).

It must also change what competitors can do after they’re chosen. Equal access to necessary system functions (including documented technical interfaces) can keep the selection from becoming cosmetic. People should be able to remove the gatekeeper’s service, move relevant data, and reverse a choice without losing basic functionality. A rule that governs only the display will not address advantages embedded elsewhere in the product. We should judge the remedy by the practical result—whether an alternative can actually become and remain the chosen service.

Finally, accountability can’t rest on the gatekeeper’s own assurances. Regulators need enough information to examine eligibility decisions, rankings, prompts, and technical restrictions (reporting should protect legitimate security and privacy interests). Independent testing can look for unequal steps or degraded functions (including changes introduced after launch). Enforcement needs consequences strong enough that evasive redesigns don’t become a routine business expense.

We call something market choice when rivals can reach people under fair conditions and a decision can take effect. A curated screen alone doesn’t establish either condition. Lawmakers and regulators should require neutral access, genuine control over defaults, functional equality, and auditable compliance—not merely a page that makes gatekeeper power look like consumer choice.","omitted":[],"refused":""}
